scope: Only frozen snapshots. Black-box supplemental probes use the original read-only WSL bubblewrap evaluator and are excluded from fixed scores.

routines.name: _ids
routines.docstring:
Validate a JSON id array and return it as a list of strings.

Shared by ``depends_on`` and ``applied`` so the two cannot drift on what
"malformed" means. Duplicates are preserved; collapsing them is a replay
concern handled in :func:`read_applied`.

routines.name: _depends_on
routines.docstring:
Return a record's dependency list, defaulting to empty.

An explicit ``null`` is malformed rather than defaulted: SPEC only gives a
default for an absent key and says non-array dependency input fails.

routines.name: read_request
routines.docstring:
Extract ``(changes, applied)`` and validate their declared shapes.

An absent ``changes`` means the request lacks a required field, which is
``invalid-request``. A present but non-array ``changes`` or ``applied`` is
a malformed *field*, reported as ``invalid-change`` per SPEC's "non-array
... dependency/journal input" clause. The distinction is what lets a
caller tell "I sent the wrong envelope" apart from "this field has the
wrong type" without guessing from the message alone.

An explicit ``applied: null`` is malformed rather than defaulted, matching
the rule for an explicit ``depends_on: null``. Unknown extra keys are
ignored: SPEC defines a required subset and does not ask the planner to
reject extensions.

routines.name: read_changes
routines.docstring:
Normalize change records to ``{"id","component","units","depends_on"}``.

Each record is validated on its own; the first bad record aborts the whole
request because a partial plan would be a deployment with unknown gaps.
``type(...) is not int`` rejects booleans. Dependencies are kept as a list
in input order because deduplication compares the dependency *set*.

routines.name: dedupe
routines.docstring:
Collapse identical records, reject conflicting duplicate IDs.

Two records sharing an ``id`` are identical when component, units and the
dependency *set* agree; dependency order and repeated names do not matter
because the graph only cares about reachability. Collapsing happens before
accounting so units are not double-counted. Any other same-id pair is
``conflicting-change``: the planner cannot tell which record the caller
meant, and picking one silently would deploy the wrong artifact.

The caller of this function must pass records already normalized by
:func:`read_changes`; it relies on ``depends_on`` being a list.

routines.name: read_applied
routines.docstring:
Return the persisted applied journal as a set of change IDs.

The journal is the caller's state of record, so this function does not
repair it. Unknown IDs are rejected later by planner (``unknown-dependency``)
once the change set is known; duplicates collapse into the set because
replay is membership and must never double-count units.

journal.py.moduleNote:
Request shape, change identity and release-journal replay.

This module is the only place that decides what a well-formed change record
is. planner consumes these plain dictionaries and must not re-derive record
shapes, otherwise two sources of truth can disagree about validity.

Import direction: standard library only. This module must never import policy,
planner or release.

routines.name: order
routines.docstring:
Return the full deterministic topological order of change IDs.

Kahn's algorithm driven by a min-heap, so among all currently eligible
changes the lexicographically smallest ID is chosen. That tie-break is what
makes the output reproducible across runs and independent of input order,
which the rollback order depends on as well.

Both graph errors are raised here because only after deduplication is the
final node set known: a dependency naming a collapsed-away or nonexistent
ID is ``unknown-dependency``, and any cycle (including one hidden in
otherwise valid input) is ``dependency-cycle`` rather than a partial plan.
A plan missing a cycle member would deploy a component whose prerequisite
never runs.

routines.name: plan
routines.docstring:
Validate, replay, order and assemble one SPEC result object.

Every rejection path returns the exact failure shape with no partial
actions, so a transport never has to merge or roll back half a plan. The
order of the checks is the order SPEC lists them: envelope, policy
(environment/action/budget), journal, graph, then the budget cap that
depends on what will actually be emitted.

comments: # Dependency sets, not lists: duplicate edges must not inflate in-degree.
# Applied is read after dedupe so unknown IDs are judged against the
# collapsed set; an ID that only existed as a duplicate is still known.
# Reverse of the *full* topological order, filtered to applied
# entries. Filtering first and reversing afterwards could invert a
# pair whose relative position depends on an unapplied change.
# Applied entries satisfy their dependencies and cost no budget, so
# they are simply not emitted.
# Plan reaches here only after the cap passed, so one accounting rule
# serves both actions: units are exactly what is emitted, and rollback
# is never truncated by budget.

Import direction is fixed: planner imports journal and policy, and neither of
those imports planner. All fallible validation is delegated outward so error
codes keep a single owner per layer; this module only adds graph-level
errors (``unknown-dependency``, ``dependency-cycle``) and the cross-layer

routines.name: check_environment_and_action
routines.docstring:
Validate environment, then that the action is a known operation.

Order matters for error reporting: SPEC lists ``invalid-environment``
before ``unsupported-action``, so an unknown environment is reported even
when the action is also unknown. G1 allows every environment/action pair;
if a later goal narrows that, the permission table belongs here rather
than in planner so planner keeps a single selection code path.

routines.name: check_budget
routines.docstring:
Return the declared budget as a plain int.

``type(x) is int`` deliberately rejects booleans: ``isinstance(True, int)``
is True in Python and SPEC says integers exclude booleans. Negative
budgets are invalid rather than clamped to zero, because a silent clamp
would turn a caller bug into an empty plan.

routines.name: check_plan_budget
routines.docstring:
Reject a plan that would emit more units than the caller allowed.

Called by planner only after replay and deduplication, because only then is
the real emitted unit count known. Checking earlier would either charge
for already-applied changes or miss collapsed duplicates. Rollback never
calls this: SPEC validates its budget field but does not cap it.

comments: # G1 spec: both environments support both operations. Keeping the table here
# rather than inline in an ``if`` means a future goal that narrows permissions
# (for example production rollback) changes this one place and both plan and
# rollback paths in planner stay untouched.
policy.py.moduleNote:
Environment, action and budget policy for the release planner.

This module is a leaf: it imports nothing from the project, so the reverse
import direction (planner -> policy) can never become a cycle. Only the
standard library is used.

comments: # Explicit UTF-8 with surrogateescape so a non-UTF-8 byte becomes a
# JSON parse error instead of an uncaught UnicodeDecodeError that would
# break the "always one JSON object, exit 0" contract.
# Serialise before printing: if a result ever held a non-JSON value, that
# is a transport bug, not a request error, and must not print half a line.
release.py.moduleNote:
JSON transport for the release planner.

Transport only: read stdin, parse JSON, hand the object to planner, print one
JSON object. This module never decides business errors and never exits
non-zero on a domain error, so callers can always parse stdout. It writes no
files and executes nothing.

routines.docstring:
Return the persisted applied journal as a set of change IDs.

The journal is the caller's state of record, so this function does not

routines.name: read_retain
routines.docstring:
Return the validated set of change IDs the caller wants kept.

G2 (CHANGE-G2 item 3), rollback only. Absent ``retain`` defaults to an
empty list; an explicit ``null`` or any non-array is malformed, matching
the rule for an explicit ``depends_on``/``applied`` null. The same
single-source ``_ids`` helper is used so ``invalid-retain`` and
``invalid-change`` cannot drift on what counts as a malformed ID array.

routines.name: check_retain_applied
routines.docstring:
Reject retain entries that are not already applied.

A retained ID absent from the journal cannot be "kept", so accepting it
would silently emit a rollback that removes nothing the caller named --
a wrong destructive plan. Reported as ``invalid-retain``, not
``unknown-dependency``: this is a retain-list problem, and the code names
the field that was wrong.

routines.docstring:
Return the full deterministic topological order of change IDs.

routines.name: retention_closure
routines.docstring:
Return retained IDs plus their applied transitive dependencies.

G2 (CHANGE-G2 item 3). A retained change keeps working only if everything
it still depends on is also left in place, so the closure walks
``depends_on`` transitively. A dependency that is *not* applied is passed
over: it is not in the rollback set at all, so it cannot be removed and
keeping it costs nothing.

Walking dependencies (not dependents) is what keeps the result minimal and
confined to applied IDs; the caller then subtracts this set from the
reverse order, leaving that order otherwise untouched.

routines.name: plan
routines.docstring:
Validate, replay, order and assemble one SPEC result object.

Every rejection path returns the exact failure shape with no partial
actions, so a transport never has to merge or roll back half a plan. The
order of the checks is the order SPEC lists them, with the G2 insertions:
envelope, policy (environment, production freeze, action, budget),
journal (applied, retain for rollback), graph, then the budget cap that
depends on what will actually be emitted.

comments: # Dependency sets, not lists: duplicate edges must not inflate in-degree.
# Environment first: G2 freezes production before anything else is
# looked at, so no later check may run (or raise) ahead of it.
# Applied is read after dedupe so unknown IDs are judged against the
# collapsed set; an ID that only existed as a duplicate is still known.
# Retain is a rollback-only field (CHANGE-G2 item 3). Plan ignores
# it entirely, so a plan request never fails on a malformed retain
# that could not affect anything it emits.
# Reverse of the *full* topological order, filtered to applied
# entries. Filtering first and reversing afterwards could invert a
# pair whose relative position depends on an unapplied change.
# Subtract the closure from the order instead of rebuilding it, so
# every surviving ID keeps its original relative position.
# Applied entries satisfy their dependencies and cost no budget, so
# they are simply not emitted.
# G2: enforce min(request budget, 3) here, after replay/dedupe, so
# the cap applies to the count actually emitted. Rollback stays
# uncapped because its budget field is validated but never enforced.
# Every rejection above raised before this point, so one accounting rule
# serves both actions: units are exactly what is emitted, and a failed
# request never reaches the assembly below.

Dependency graph, deterministic ordering and result assembly.

routines.name: check_environment_and_action
routines.docstring:
Validate environment, freeze production, then check the action.

Order matters for error reporting: SPEC lists ``invalid-environment``
before ``unsupported-action``, so an unknown environment is reported even
when the action is also unknown. G2 narrows the permission table to
staging only; that rule lives here, not in planner.

routines.name: check_budget
routines.docstring:
Return the declared budget as a plain int.

``type(x) is int`` deliberately rejects booleans: ``isinstance(True, int)``
is True in Python and SPEC says integers exclude booleans. Negative
budgets are invalid rather than clamped to zero, because a silent clamp
would turn a caller bug into an empty plan.

routines.name: check_plan_budget
routines.docstring:
Reject a plan that would emit more units than the caller allowed.

Called by planner only after replay and deduplication, because only then is
the real emitted unit count known. Checking earlier would either charge
for already-applied changes or miss collapsed duplicates. ``budget`` must
be the effective value from :func:`effective_plan_budget`, not the raw
request value, or the G2 staging cap is silently bypassed. Rollback never
calls this: SPEC validates its budget field but does not cap it.

routines.name: effective_plan_budget
routines.docstring:
Return the plan quota actually enforced for this release.

G2 (CHANGE-G2 item 2): a staging plan may never exceed
``STAGING_PLAN_CAP`` even when the request budget is larger; only the
smaller value counts. Keeping the cap here means planner carries one
enforced number instead of comparing against the raw request. Callers must
not apply this to rollback, which stays uncapped.

comments: # Actions the planner understands at all; whether one is allowed in a given
# environment is a separate permission question decided below.
# G2 release policy: production is frozen for *both* actions. Kept as data so
# planner never spells an environment name itself.
# G2 staging plan quota. The effective plan budget is min(request, this cap);
# rollback is deliberately exempt (CHANGE-G2 item 2/3).
# G2 (CHANGE-G2 item 1): production is frozen as soon as the environment is
# known, *before* any change/dependency/graph validation, so a malformed
# graph on production still reports ``production-frozen`` rather than a
# graph error. Deciding this in policy is what guarantees no downstream
# layer can emit partial actions for production; both actions are frozen,
# so the check deliberately precedes the action lookup.

routines.name: _string_list
routines.docstring:
Strict ``list[str]`` check.

``str`` is rejected explicitly because it is iterable; without this guard a
caller sending ``"depends_on": "abc"`` would silently become ``["a","b","c"]``
and produce bogus dependencies instead of ``invalid-change``.

routines.name: read_changes
routines.docstring:
Validate ``changes`` and collapse duplicates.

Returns a list of canonical ``{"id","component","units","depends_on"}`` dicts
in first-seen order. Duplicates are compared by id/component/units and the
*set* of dependencies: dependency order carries no meaning for the graph
because the topological order is derived from the graph itself, so
``["b","a"]`` and ``["a","b"]`` must not be treated as a second record.

routines.name: read_applied
routines.docstring: Validate the caller-supplied applied journal (defaults to empty).

routines.name: verify_known
routines.docstring:
Reject dependency targets or applied entries that name no declared change.

Done before cycle detection: a missing target is an input mistake, while a
cycle is a structural one. Reporting ``unknown-dependency`` first keeps the
error code stable regardless of the (dict-ordered) traversal.

comments: # A self-dependency is not rejected here: it is a one-node cycle and must
# be reported as ``dependency-cycle`` by the graph layer, not as a
# malformed record.
journal.py.moduleNote:
Normalize release records at the input boundary.

This module owns the *identity* of a change and the *persisted release journal*
supplied by the caller. It never looks at the graph topology and never makes a
policy decision: it only turns untrusted JSON into a canonical set of records or
raises ``conflicting-change`` / ``invalid-change`` / ``unknown-dependency``.

routines.name: failure
routines.docstring: The only permitted failure shape. Never carries partial actions.

routines.name: dependency_edges
routines.docstring:
Map id -> dependency ids, rejecting self-loops as cycles.

Self-dependency is reported as ``dependency-cycle`` (a one-node cycle)
rather than ``unknown-dependency``: the target does exist, it is just
impossible to satisfy.

routines.name: topological_order
routines.docstring:
Kahn's algorithm, always expanding the lexicographically smallest ready id.

Why a heap of *currently eligible* nodes instead of "sort the final list":
the tie-break rule is defined over the ready set at each step. A node made
eligible late by a small-id dependency may therefore precede a node that was
ready earlier but sorts after it. Sorting afterwards would produce a
different (still valid, but non-conforming) order.

Ordering is Python's own string order (code point), identical on every
platform; ids themselves are compared, never their hashes, so the result does
not depend on insertion or hash order.

routines.name: plan
routines.docstring: Validate, order, replay and assemble the result for one request.

comments: # Build reverse edges over the *deduplicated* dependency set. A record may list
# the same dependency twice (``["a","a"]``); iterating the raw list would add
# ``dependent`` to ``dependents["a"]`` twice, and the second ``discard`` on the
# already-satisfied node would be a no-op that still consumes an entry -- a
# valid plan would then be misreported as a cycle.
# Anything still blocked is on (or downstream of) a cycle. Self-loops were
# caught earlier, but leaving the generic check here keeps the invariant
# local: "fewer ordered nodes than nodes" means a cycle, always.
# Duplicate ids were collapsed in journal.read_changes, so this dict is a
# faithful 1:1 map; an applied id naming a dropped duplicate still resolves.
# Already applied entries are *replayed*: they satisfy dependencies but are
# not re-emitted, so their units do not count against the budget.
# Budget is checked against what is actually emitted, after
# deduplication and replay -- not against the whole change list.
# rollback: the reverse of the *full* deterministic order, filtered to applied
# entries. Reversing the full order (rather than ordering only the applied
# subset) matters: an applied change must still be undone after everything it
# depends on, even though the intermediate unapplied changes are skipped.
# The budget field was validated above but deliberately does not cap a
# rollback: SPEC requires a full undo regardless of remaining budget.
planner.py.moduleNote:
Compose policy and journal data into a plan.

Responsibilities: build the dependency graph, produce the single deterministic
topological order, replay the applied journal against it, and assemble the one
result object the transport layer prints. All input validation already happened
in ``journal``/``policy``; anything raised here is structural.

routines.name: read_action
routines.docstring: Validate environment and action; returns the action string.

routines.name: read_budget
routines.docstring:
Validate the budget field; returns it unchanged.

``type(...) is int`` (not ``isinstance``) is deliberate: ``True``/``False``
are ints in Python and SPEC forbids booleans as integers. The value is then
*interpreted* by the planner, because whether it caps the plan depends on the
action: ``rollback`` validates it but must not be capped by it.

routines.name: limit_for
routines.docstring: Backwards-compatible helper: validate policy and return the budget.

comments: # G1 promotes rollback for both environments. Keeping the action check in the
# policy layer (rather than in the planner) is what preserves the transport
# contract ``unsupported-action`` for anything else, including future G2 actions
# that are still gated by an incarnation flag. Tuples, not sets: membership tests
# on a set raise TypeError for unhashable JSON values (e.g. ``["plan"]``).
# ``in`` on a frozenset raises TypeError for unhashable input such as a list,
# which would escape as a crash instead of a domain error. Compare by type
# first so every value maps to a SPEC code.

Validate release policy before computing actions.

Policy answers three questions and nothing else: which environments exist,
which actions the *current goal* supports, and what the budget means. It never
inspects changes, so it cannot leak a partial plan on its own.

routines.name: read_applied
routines.docstring: Validate the caller-supplied applied journal (defaults to empty).

routines.name: read_retain
routines.docstring:
Validate the rollback ``retain`` list (G2-3); returns its canonical set.

``retain`` names already-applied changes that must *not* be rolled back.
Everything about it is a structural/journal property, which is why it lives
next to ``read_applied`` rather than in the planner:

* ``None``/absent -> empty (the caller sent no pinned set). Unlike
  ``depends_on`` there is no "default" to fold, so the planner passes the raw
  value; ``read_retain`` also accepts the absent case as ``None``.
* Must be a list of strings, each naming an entry of ``applied``. A list
  holding a not-applied id is rejected here, not silently ignored: the caller
  asked to keep something the journal does not have, and proceeding would
  quietly roll it back anyway -- the worst possible failure for the one thing
  this field exists to protect.
* Duplicates are *collapsed*, not rejected: a repeated id means the same
  pinned change, and rejecting it would make an otherwise harmless idempotent
  retry fail. Order is irrelevant because the planner recomputes the order.
* Unknown ids cannot reach this point: ``verify_known`` already guarantees
  every ``applied`` id exists, and this check requires subset of ``applied``.

# ``invalid-change`` would tell the caller to look at their change records.

routines.name: retained_closure
routines.docstring:
Expand a validated ``retain`` to everything it transitively needs (G2-3).

Kept because a retained change is kept *installed*, so the things it depends
on must stay installed too -- rolling a dependency back under a live
dependent would leave a broken deployment. Two deliberate boundaries:

* Only *applied* dependencies join the closure. A dependency that was never
  applied is, by construction, not in the rollback set at all (rollback only
  emits applied ids), so adding it would do nothing but inflate ``units``.
  It is also the reason this cannot simply be ``retain`` closed over the raw
  graph: an unapplied intermediate must not resurrect its own applied
  ancestors. Example: retained ``d`` -> unapplied ``b`` -> applied ``a``;
  ``a`` is *not* retained, because ``d`` was never actually deployed on top
  of ``a`` through the current graph. This is the single most non-obvious
  rule of the change and is covered by a dedicated test.
* Walk over the *normalized* edges (``dependency_edges`` output), which are
  already validated: no gaps, no cycles, so the loop terminates and every id
  resolved. Idempotent by construction (``while`` re-queues nothing that is
  already in the set), so a diamond closes once.

routines.name: rollback_actions
routines.docstring:
The G2-3 rollback order: applied, not retained, reverse topological.

Reverse of the *full* deterministic order (not of the applied subset), so an
undone change is still undone after everything it depends on even when
unapplied changes sit in between. Filtering by ``applied_ids`` and then by the
retained closure is the only difference from G1's rollback: no re-sorting, so
everything outside ``retain`` keeps its exact G1 position.

routines.name: plan
routines.docstring: Validate, order, replay and assemble the result for one request.

comments: # Build reverse edges over the *deduplicated* dependency set. A record may list
# the same dependency twice (``["a","a"]``); iterating the raw list would add
# ``dependent`` to ``dependents["a"]`` twice, and the second ``discard`` on the
# already-satisfied node would be a no-op that still consumes an entry -- a
# valid plan would then be misreported as a cycle.
# Anything still blocked is on (or downstream of) a cycle. Self-loops were
# caught earlier, but leaving the generic check here keeps the invariant
# local: "fewer ordered nodes than nodes" means a cycle, always.
# The environment gate (including ``production-frozen``) runs first on
# purpose: G2 freezes production before graph/change validation, so this
# ordering is what makes a malformed production request still answer
# ``production-frozen`` instead of ``invalid-change``/``dependency-cycle``.
# Duplicate ids were collapsed in journal.read_changes, so this dict is a
# faithful 1:1 map; an applied id naming a dropped duplicate still resolves.
# ``retain`` is read only for rollback: G2 scopes it to rollback, and a
# plan request that happens to carry the field (even a malformed one) must
# behave exactly as it did in G1 rather than start failing validation.
# Already applied entries are *replayed*: they satisfy dependencies but are
# not re-emitted, so their units do not count against the budget.
# G2-2: a staging plan is judged against ``min(budget, 3)``. The cap is
# applied to the *emitted* total, after deduplication and replay -- i.e.
# exactly where G1 compared against the raw budget -- so replay keeps its
# old meaning and only the ceiling changes.
# Still checked against what is actually emitted, not against the whole
# change list, and still all-or-nothing: no partial actions.
# rollback: the reverse of the *full* deterministic order, filtered to applied
# entries and then to the retained closure (retain + applied transitive deps).
# Reversing the full order (rather than ordering only the applied subset)
# matters: an applied change must still be undone after everything it depends
# on, even though the intermediate unapplied changes are skipped.
# The budget field was validated above but deliberately does not cap a
# rollback: SPEC G1 requires a full undo regardless of remaining budget, and
# G2's cap is explicitly a *staging plan* limit only.

Compose policy and journal data into a plan.

Responsibilities: enforce the environment gate, build the dependency graph,
produce the single deterministic topological order, replay the applied journal
against it, compute the retained closure of a rollback, and assemble the one
result object the transport layer prints. All input validation already happened

routines.name: read_budget

``type(...) is int`` (not ``isinstance``) is deliberate: ``True``/``False``
are ints in Python and SPEC forbids booleans as integers. The validated value
is *interpreted* by the caller, because what it caps depends on the action:
``rollback`` validates it but must not be capped, and a plan is capped by

routines.name: effective_budget
routines.docstring:
The budget a staging plan is actually judged against (G2-2).

``min`` rather than "reject budgets above 3": the request may legitimately
over-ask (e.g. a shared caller default of 100); only the emitted units decide
whether the cap was exceeded. Already-applied entries are handled later by the
planner and never reach this cap, so replay keeps its G1 semantics.

Kept for the G1 unit test and any embedded caller. It returns the request

comments: # G1 promoted rollback for both environments; G2 keeps both actions but freezes
# the whole production environment (see below). Keeping the action check in the
# policy layer (rather than in the planner) is what preserves the transport
# contract ``unsupported-action`` for anything else. Tuples, not sets: membership
# tests on a set raise TypeError for unhashable JSON values (e.g. ``["plan"]``).

# before any graph or change validation, so a malformed graph in production still
# yields ``production-frozen`` and never a partial action list.
# G2-2: the effective budget of a staging plan is ``min(request budget, 3)``.
# A request that asks for more than 3 is *not* an error by itself -- only trying
# to emit more than 3 units is ``budget-exceeded``, which is what makes this a
# cap rather than a new validation rule. Rollback is not capped (G1 rule kept);

Return the rollback `retain` set, defaulting to empty.

widened. The error is `invalid-retain`, distinct from the journal's

Validate the persisted ``applied`` journal and resolve it to a set of IDs.

``applied`` is the raw value from the request or ``MISSING`` when the key
was absent. An explicit JSON ``null`` is NOT a default: it is a malformed

routines.docstring:

A dependency naming an ID absent from the change array is an incomplete
graph: it cannot be ordered or planned, so it fails as ``unknown-dependency``.

comments: # Every string is a valid ID, including "id"/"component"/"units" and
# leading-underscore names, so records must never be stashed inside the input
# dict to detect duplicates. read_changes only needs to *look up* a candidate by
# ID, so no synthetic key is ever stored. This spelling is still rejected as an
# ID so it can never become an alias if that ever changes.
# Sentinel for "the caller omitted this field", because JSON null is a distinct,
# malformed value that must not be conflated with an absent key.
# Synthetic-ID guard: this private spelling is reserved by the module, so
# an ID using it could alias internal bookkeeping if that is ever added.
# Rejecting it is sound: it is never a legitimate caller ID here.
# Booleans are ints in Python; the spec excludes them, so compare types.
# A string is not a JSON integer: reject it rather than coerce, otherwise
# the journal's identity/dedup would depend on a hidden conversion.
# One bad record anywhere rejects the whole array: no partial journal.
# The id is also an ID string subject to the same reservation.
# An explicit null is malformed, not "default": only absence defaults.
# Same ID, different content: the journal cannot tell which release
# is meant, so this is a hard conflict rather than a merge.
# Only a genuinely absent key defaults to an empty journal.

routines.name: read_retain
routines.docstring:
Validate ``retain`` (CHANGE-G2.3) and return it as a set of IDs.

``retain`` is only meaningful for rollback. Rules and the reason for each:

* absent      -> empty set. CHANGE-G2.3: "accepts `retain`, default empty".
* ``plan``    -> the *key* must be absent, whatever its value. "Applies only
  to rollback", so a plan that carries it is rejected as ``invalid-retain``
  rather than silently ignored -- otherwise a caller could believe a change
  was protected on the plan path and it never was. Keyed on presence, not on
  the value, so ``retain: []`` on a plan is rejected too.
* non-array   -> ``invalid-retain``. Note an explicit JSON ``null`` is NOT
  the default (same rule as ``applied``): only absence defaults.
* each item   -> must be a nonempty string, not a bool/int/list/dict.
  ``type(item) is not str`` rather than ``isinstance`` so subclasses and
  numeric look-alikes cannot coerce; booleans in particular are ints.
* unknown ID  -> ``invalid-retain``. It cannot be "already applied", so it
  is rejected up front instead of being ignored as a no-op.
* not applied -> ``invalid-retain``. CHANGE-G2.3 defines retain as IDs that
  are *already applied*; retaining an unapplied change is a caller bug.
* duplicates  -> harmless: the result is a set.

``applied`` must already be resolved by :func:`read_applied`, so retain IDs
are checked against the persisted journal, not the raw request. Callers pass
``MISSING`` when the request has no ``retain`` key at all.

routines.name: retained_closure
routines.docstring:
IDs that must survive a rollback: ``retain`` plus applied dependencies.

CHANGE-G2.3: "Retain the transitive dependencies that are applied and
required by those retained changes." Two boundaries are deliberate:

* The walk *stops at non-applied nodes.* A dependency that is not applied
  was never released, so there is nothing to protect, and the changes behind
  it are not "applied and required" on that path.
* The walk is only over dependency edges, never over dependents: retaining
  ``c`` does not force retaining an unrelated node that merely happens to
  sit later in the order.

The change itself is included; ``retain`` is already a subset of ``applied``
(journal.read_retain enforces it), so the closure is a subset of ``applied``
and can be subtracted from the rollback emission directly.

routines.docstring: Entry point used by the transport; keeps every request JSON-answerable.

comments: # Single failure constructor for every error path: a fresh object with empty
# actions and zero units, so a half-built plan can never leak ("never emit
# partial actions"). Do not let callers pass a partially filled list here.
# Units are derived from the emitted changes, never from an earlier total:
# after retain-removal or replay filtering only what is really emitted bills.
# Any node never released from a dependency is on, or behind, a cycle.
# Cycles are rejected for both actions: the journal itself is unusable,
# even when plan would not emit the offending node.
# Order here is the observable contract (ARCHITECTURE.md section 3):
# envelope + freeze + cap, then records/journal, then graph, cycle,
# retain, and only then billing. production-frozen must beat every
# graph/change error below, while invalid-environment/-action/-budget
# stay in front of it.
# A missing "applied" key defaults to an empty journal; an explicit null
# must not (see journal.read_applied), hence the MISSING sentinel.
# Billing happens *after* replay filtering (already-applied changes are
# free) and against policy.cap, which policy.decide already reduced to
# min(request budget, 3) for staging plans. The comparison is strict:
# a plan of exactly `cap` units fits, cap+1 does not. Nothing is emitted
# on excess, not even the actions that did fit.
# Rollback: reverse of the FULL order, not of the applied subgraph. Relative
# order forced by a non-applied node still applies, so this list is the
# original deterministic reverse order, with only retained IDs removed.
# No budget check: the budget was validated in policy.decide but must never
# cap rollback (SPEC.md, kept by CHANGE-G2.3 which only adds retain).
# Last line of defence: an unexpected bug must still yield one JSON
# object, because release.py promises "exit normally with a JSON
# result". It must not be the common path -- add a test if it fires.
planner.py.moduleNote:
Compose policy and journal data into a plan.

Owns the deterministic graph order, the G2 retained closure, plan billing and
the exact result objects. It never re-validates raw record shapes; that belongs
to journal/policy.

routines.name: decide
routines.docstring: Validate the request envelope and return a :class:`Policy`.

comments: # Action *names* the dispatcher understands. Keeping this independent of the
# environment lets policy distinguish "no such action" (unsupported-action) from
# "that action is frozen here" (production-frozen) without hard-coding either
# in the planner.
# CHANGE-G2.1: this release is staging-only. Production plan *and* rollback are
# frozen even when the graph is malformed. A frozen request must never emit
# partial actions, so this check runs before any graph/change/retain work and
# planner builds no action list until policy has returned.
# CHANGE-G2.2: staging plan effective budget is the smaller of the request
# budget and this hard ceiling. It is a staging *plan* rule, not a transport
# rule, so it is not applied to rollback (whose budget is validated by type and
# range but never caps the emitted units).
# G2 freezes production; it does not remove or rename actions. An
# unknown action therefore stays `unsupported-action` in *both*
# environments, ahead of the freeze: G1's "action before budget"
# precedence is part of SPEC.md and is not superseded by CHANGE-G2.
# Booleans are ints in Python; `True`/`False` must not pass as a budget.
# Budget is validated before the freeze because a malformed budget is a
# transport/policy error; CHANGE-G2 only moves the freeze ahead of *graph
# and change* validation (invalid-change, conflicts, unknown ids, cycles,
# retain, billing). No action can be emitted on either path.
# The cap is applied exactly once, here, so the planner cannot
# accidentally bill a staging plan against the raw (larger) request
# budget. `min` (not replace) keeps a tighter request budget in force.
# Rollback: the cap is unused, and billing is never checked against it.
policy.py.moduleNote:
Validate release policy before computing actions.

Owns environment, action and budget policy only: which environments and actions
exist, the budget envelope, the G2 production freeze and the G2 staging plan
cap. Validation order here is observable and must not be reshuffled:

    environment -> action -> budget envelope -> production freeze

Replay, identity, graph, retain and ordering stay in journal/planner.

release.py.moduleNote:
JSON transport for the release planner.

Transport only: read one JSON request from stdin, hand it to the planner and
print exactly one JSON object. Every request, including domain errors and
malformed input, exits normally.
